messages.subject: Issues with readMSIData
messages.body_plain:
Dear Cardinalers,

I am attempting to import a new MSI dataset into Cardinal, however I keep on getting an import error that I believe is due to the binning in Cardinal:

data <- readImzML(file, folder=getwd(), attach.only = F, mass.accuracy = 1, units.accuracy = c("ppm"))

Error in validObject(.Object) :
  invalid class "Hashmat" object: elements of keys must be unique

I have tried to adjust the mass accuracy units and I have used the function readMSIData with no prevail.

The one thing that does work is to change the accuracy units to "mz" values. However, I would like to keep the "ppm" call.

Has anyone else come across this error and can explain why it is occurring?

Thank you!

Maggie

P.S. of interest - using previous datasets I have had success with the same command ... puzzling.

messages.subject: Re: Issues with readMSIData
messages.body_plain:
Hi Maggie,

For units.accuracy=ppm, try using a larger value for mass.accuracy.

The m/z values are rounded and converted to strings to make column names, and the step size is probably too small for the resulting names to be unique.

I need to revisit the code for converting m/z values to column names at some point since I think it's probably rounding too aggressively, but for now a larger value for mass.accuracy when using units.accuracy=ppm should solve the problem.

-Kylie

As far as I can see the selected method (is the correct one?) is some subjetive and it depends on the user opinion and his/her experience and if the data is convenient.

How can we construct a custom normalization method in an easy way? That is, if you want to normalize by RMS apply this function to normalize, if you want to normalize by mean apply this, if you want the median apply this.

Regards!

messages.subject: Re: Custom normalization method/Normalization methods available
messages.body_plain:
Currently, only TIC is implemented, but it's relatively straightforward to use a custom normalization function. All of the preprocessing methods in Cardinal are designed to accept a user-written function in place of the pre-implemented ones in their "method=" argument.

Each of the help pages details the precise arguments needed for the user-written processing function to be applied to each spectrum properly (see "Details" under ?normalize, for example, which allows any function of the form function(x, ...) where 'x' is a vector of intensities).

I do plan to add more pre-implemented normalization methods. I have mostly been working on improving support for large datasets, so I have not gotten a chance yet. Letting me know which methods would be most useful and posting links to articles that describe their implementation is most helpful to me in deciding what to add. :-)

-Kylie

messages.subject: Re: filter by intensity
messages.body_plain:
Hi Suhyung,

It sounds like you want to subset the dataset to remove a region of unnecessary pixels. To do this, you can simply subset the whole object using the bracket operators. You can do this either in an automated way if you have some kind of rule for deciding which pixels you wish to retain, or manually if you would like to select by hand.

For the former, you could do something like:

keep <- pixelApply(msset, function(x) all(x > 1))
msset2 <- msset[,keep]

which would first create a logical vector of the pixels with mass spectra where all intensities are > 1 (or whatever rule you want to apply), and then subset the whole dataset to contain only those pixels.

Or to select the region you wish to keep manually, you can do:

keep <- select(msset, mz=500)
msset2 <- msset[,keep]

where you set mz= to whatever ion image is most helpful in selecting the region of interest you want to keep. This allows you to manually select the vertices of a polygonal region of the image.

I hope one of these helps.

-Kylie

Hi Kylie,
thanks for your reply.
Well, I was thinking in some sort of "quality evaluation" by doing a replicate of the excellent job developed by Deininger et al in 2011 (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3124646/pdf/216_2011_Article_4929.pdf).
They tried a lot of normalization methods and I think that for analysis refinement the application of these methods would be ideal in Cardinal.
By doing these comparisons of some of them and looking their effect in your data set you can see what normalization method is adjusting in a better way under your experimental conditions (ie. figure attached)
Some other articles citing different normalization methods I've seen:

- Sliding Window Normalization (SWN): https://academic.oup.com/bioinformatics/article-lookup/doi/10.1093/bioinformatics/btv356. A different approach developed in 2015.
- Similar work to Deininger but developed in Matlab: http://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ac201767g. Very interesting.
- Variance-stabilizing normalization for improved information recovery: http://www.pnas.org/content/111/3/1216.full.pdf

Cheers
Edu
